chunks.document_content: Open Access Information sources A comprehensive literature search was conducted in PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library from database inception to 31 Decem­ ber 2025. Two reviewers performed the search indepen­ dently. To ensure completeness, the reference lists of all included studies and of relevant systematic reviews and meta-analyses were also screened manually. Any disagreements were resolved through discussion and consensus. Search strategy The search strategy combined Medical Subject Head­ ings (MeSH), Emtree terms, and free-text keywords. No publication-date or language restrictions were applied. Reviews, editorials, comments, and letters were excluded. The following terms were used: Study selection and data extraction Study selection and data extraction were performed inde­ pendently by two authors using the Rayyan web appli­ cation. Titles and abstracts of all retrieved records were screened initially, and any study considered potentially relevant by either reviewer proceeded to full-text assess­ ment. Full texts were then reviewed to determine eligi­ bility according to the predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria. Any discrepancies between reviewers were resolved by consultation with a third author. (fetal OR fetus) AND (cardiac OR heart) AND (inter­ vention OR procedure OR surgery OR therapy OR "intrauterine intervention" OR "in utero intervention" OR "fetal cardiac intervention" OR FCI) AND ("aortic valvuloplasty" OR "pulmonary valvuloplasty" OR "atrial septoplasty" OR "balloon valvuloplasty" OR "fetal aortic valvuloplasty" OR "fetal pulmonary valvuloplasty" OR FAV OR FPV OR FASI) NOT (review OR editorial OR comment OR letter). For all studies meeting eligibility criteria, data were extracted independently and in duplicate, including study design, population characteristics, type of fetal cardiac intervention, comparator group, and reported clini­ cal outcomes. Extracted outcomes included established measures of gestational and postnatal prognosis relevant to fetal cardiac intervention. Consensus was reached through discussion when differences occurred, ensuring accuracy and completeness of the final dataset. When necessary, authors were contacted to clarify ambiguous reporting or obtain missing information. Cases that did not report outcome data (e.g., BVC, live birth, or post­ natal death) were excluded from analyses of the corre­ sponding endpoint. The detailed search strategies for each database, includ­ ing subject headings (e.g., MeSH and Emtree), are pro­ vided in Appendix S1. Definitions of clinical outcomes and procedural stratification Clinical outcomes were defined prior to analysis to ensure consistency across studies. Technical success was defined according to each original publication; however, in general, it reflected successful balloon inflation across the target valve with improvement in antegrade flow. For FAV, this typically corresponded to balloon inflation across the aortic valve with demonstrable enhancement of antegrade aortic flow. BVC was defined as a post­ natal circulation supported by separate functional left and right ventricles. When multiple time points were reported, outcomes at hospital discharge were priori­ tized. If discharge data were unavailable, the outcome as reported in the study was used. When the timing of BVC assessment was not specified, the reported value was accepted as final. Live birth was defined as an infant alive at the time of delivery. Postnatal death referred to mor­ tality occurring between birth and hospital discharge.

chunks.document_content: Statistical analysis Given the presence of a competing event (transplantation), a competing risks analysis was performed, considering death as the event of interest and transplantation as the competing event. Associations between covariates and mortality were evaluated using the Fine-Gray subdistribution hazards model, which es­ timates the effect of covariates on the cumulative incidence of the event of interest in the presence of competing risks. Multivariable models were adjusted for age, sex, and IABP use, and were intentionally parsimonious given the limited number of events to avoid overfitting. Results are presented as sub­ distribution hazard ratios (SHR) with 95% confidence intervals. The proportional hazards assumption was assessed by testing interactions between covariates and time; when violations were identified, time-dependent effects were modeled using interac­ tion terms with follow-up time, and results are reported as SHR for the baseline effect and for the time-varying component (TVC SHR). Given the advanced clinical status of the study population, particular attention was paid to avoid overadjustment. Variables included in multivariable models were selected based on clin­ ical relevance and statistical criteria, acknowledging the po­ tential overlap between frailty measures and markers of disease severity, which may share common underlying pathways.

chunks.document_content: Open Access Eluted peptides were analyzed on an Orbitrap Explo­ ris 480 mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific) equipped with a nano-electrospray ionization source. The spray voltage was set to 2.3 kV, and high-field asymmetric waveform ion mobility spectrometry was applied using compensation voltages of - 70 V and - 45 V. Full MS scans were acquired in the Orbitrap analyzer at a resolu­ tion of 60,000 across an m/z range of 400-1,200. Tandem MS/MS spectra were acquired at a resolution of 30,000 with the first mass fixed at m/z 110. TurboTMT mode was disabled to maintain compatibility with label-free quantification. The top 15 most intense precursor ions were selected for higher-energy collisional dissociation with a normalized collision energy of 27%, and dynamic exclusion was set to 30 s. The automatic gain control tar­ get was set to 75%, with an intensity threshold of 10,000 ions/s and a maximum injection time of 100 ms. During hospitalization, all participants provided writ­ ten informed consent permitting the use of their blood samples for non-genetic experimental analyses. Compre­ hensive clinical data, including demographic character­ istics, comorbidities, vital signs, laboratory parameters, echocardiographic measurements, and medication use, were systematically collected from electronic medical records. Peripheral venous blood samples were obtained, and plasma was isolated by centrifugation and stored at -80 °C until analysis. Samples were transported on dry ice to Jingjie PTM BioLabs (Hangzhou, China) for label-free quantitative proteomic profiling. To reduce the interference of highly abundant plasma proteins, such as albumin and immunoglobulins, on downstream mass spectrometry-based analyses, plasma samples were depleted using PierceTM Top 14 Abundant Protein Depletion Spin Columns (Thermo Scientific) in strict accordance with the manufacturer's protocol. Briefly, frozen plasma aliquots were thawed on ice and centrifuged at 12,000 × g for 10 min at 4 °C to remove cellular debris. The clarified supernatant was transferred to fresh tubes and subjected to high-abundance protein depletion. Protein concentrations in the depleted frac­ tions were quantified using a bicinchoninic acid (BCA) assay, with all standards and samples measured in techni­ cal triplicates (Additional file 1: Table S1). Equal amounts of total protein were subsequently used for enzymatic digestion to ensure comparability across samples. Deple­ tion efficiency and protein integrity were evaluated by sodium dodecyl sulfate-polyacrylamide gel electropho­ resis (SDS-PAGE) before and after depletion (Additional file 1: Figure S2), and only samples demonstrating satis­ factory depletion efficiency and intact protein profiles were advanced for LC-MS/MS analysis. Samples with visible hemolysis or flagged as having a high risk of pre-analytical bias were excluded. Raw MS/MS data were processed using Proteome Dis­ coverer software (version 2.4.1.15). Spectra were searched against the Homo_sapiens_9606_PR_20201214.fasta database (75,777 entries), concatenated with a reverse decoy database to enable false discovery rate (FDR) esti­ mation. Trypsin was specified as the proteolytic enzyme, allowing up to two missed cleavages. The minimum pep­ tide length was set to six amino acids, and up to three variable modifications per peptide were permitted. Pre­ cursor mass tolerance was set at 10 ppm, and fragment ion tolerance at 0.02 Da.

chunks.document_content: Similar uncertainties exist for FASI and FPV in their respective indications [3, 4, 12]. Previous meta-analyses frequently relied on single-arm studies without an internal control group or on non- arm-based comparisons, in which outcomes for FCI and expectant management were extracted from different studies [3, 13-15]. Such approaches are inherently vul­ nerable to confounding and cannot adequately account for differences in baseline disease severity, case selection, and centre-specific practice patterns. To address these gaps, we conducted a primary meta-analysis restricted to cohorts in which FCI and expect­ ant management were compared within the same study population. A separate exploratory technical-success analysis additionally included FAV cohorts with extract­ able successful-versus-unsuccessful outcomes. Outcomes were pooled across independent cohorts to obtain more precise comparative estimates. To our knowledge, this is the first meta-analysis restricted to within-study com­ parisons of FCI and expectant management and the first quantitative synthesis of FAV outcomes according to We excluded case reports, conference abstracts, retracted publications, and studies in which outcome data for the relevant fetal cardiac condition could not be extracted separately. Overlapping reports that did not contribute unique analysis-specific data were excluded. When an overlapping report provided eligible data for a distinct secondary analysis, it was retained as an included report only for that analysis, did not add an independent study population, and was not pooled simultaneously with the overlapping report. stratified by procedure type (FAV, FPV, or FASI). For FAV, pairwise subgroup comparisons were conducted between (i) technical success vs. expectant management, (ii) tech­ nical failure vs. expectant management, and (iii) technical success vs. technical failure, where data were available. For comparative meta-analyses, postnatal death was ana­ lyzed using the number of live-born infants with known postnatal vital status in each study arm as the denomina­ tor. Fetuses that did not result in live birth were excluded from the postnatal-death risk set. Outcome availability was assessed separately for each study arm and endpoint. Studies or study arms lacking extractable comparative data for a given outcome were excluded only from that endpoint-specific meta-analysis. Cohort-level numera­ tors, denominators, and reasons for non-inclusion in individual outcome analyses are reported in Table 1.

Spectra were searched against the Homo_sapiens_9606_PR_20201214.fasta database (75,777 entries), concatenated with a reverse decoy database to enable false discovery rate (FDR) esti­ mation. Trypsin was specified as the proteolytic enzyme, allowing up to two missed cleavages. The minimum pep­ tide length was set to six amino acids, and up to three variable modifications per peptide were permitted. Pre­ cursor mass tolerance was set at 10 ppm, and fragment ion tolerance at 0.02 Da.

chunks.document_content: Similar uncertainties exist for FASI and FPV in their respective indications [3, 4, 12]. Previous meta-analyses frequently relied on single-arm studies without an internal control group or on non- arm-based comparisons, in which outcomes for FCI and expectant management were extracted from different studies [3, 13-15]. Such approaches are inherently vul­ nerable to confounding and cannot adequately account for differences in baseline disease severity, case selection, and centre-specific practice patterns. To address these gaps, we conducted a primary meta-analysis restricted to cohorts in which FCI and expect­ ant management were compared within the same study population. A separate exploratory technical-success analysis additionally included FAV cohorts with extract­ able successful-versus-unsuccessful outcomes. Outcomes were pooled across independent cohorts to obtain more precise comparative estimates. To our knowledge, this is the first meta-analysis restricted to within-study com­ parisons of FCI and expectant management and the first quantitative synthesis of FAV outcomes according to We excluded case reports, conference abstracts, retracted publications, and studies in which outcome data for the relevant fetal cardiac condition could not be extracted separately. Overlapping reports that did not contribute unique analysis-specific data were excluded. When an overlapping report provided eligible data for a distinct secondary analysis, it was retained as an included report only for that analysis, did not add an independent study population, and was not pooled simultaneously with the overlapping report. stratified by procedure type (FAV, FPV, or FASI). For FAV, pairwise subgroup comparisons were conducted between (i) technical success vs. expectant management, (ii) tech­ nical failure vs. expectant management, and (iii) technical success vs. technical failure, where data were available. For comparative meta-analyses, postnatal death was ana­ lyzed using the number of live-born infants with known postnatal vital status in each study arm as the denomina­ tor. Fetuses that did not result in live birth were excluded from the postnatal-death risk set. Outcome availability was assessed separately for each study arm and endpoint. Studies or study arms lacking extractable comparative data for a given outcome were excluded only from that endpoint-specific meta-analysis. Cohort-level numera­ tors, denominators, and reasons for non-inclusion in individual outcome analyses are reported in Table 1.
